tip: For she in reported speech use ‘ei bod hi’: ‘dywedodd Siân ei bod hi'n mynd’ = Siân said she was going.
For he in reported speech use ‘ei fod e’: ‘ei fod e'n symud’ = that he was moving.
‘cael’ plus a possessive forms the passive: ‘yn cael eu hadrodd’ = are told, literally get their telling.
In ‘wedi'i gynnwys’, ‘wedi’ plus ‘'i’ marks a passive: has been included, and the ‘'i’ soft-mutates the verb to ‘gynnwys’.
‘mae angen ymbarél’ means an umbrella is needed. ‘mae angen’ plus a noun expresses a need, with no separate word for a.
Reported speech uses ‘bod’, not the plain verb: ‘ei bod hi’ means that she, so ‘ei bod hi wedi penderfynu’ = that she had decided.
And is normally ‘ac’ before a vowel and ‘a’ before a consonant. Here ‘amser ac arian’ = time and money, ‘ac’ because ‘arian’ starts with a vowel.
‘a’ opens an indirect yes or no question: ‘a oeddwn i wedi gorffen’ = whether I had finished.
‘dod â’ is literally come with and means to bring: ‘yn dod â llawenydd’ = bringing joy.
Fronting the subject adds emphasis: ‘y ci sy wedi bwyta’ puts the dog first, and ‘sy’ means the one that has.
‘ei’ meaning her aspirate-mutates a following t to th: ‘talent’ becomes ‘ei thalent’.
The superlative ends in ‘-a’ or ‘-af’: ‘hardda’ = prettiest, formed from ‘hardd’.
‘tri’, meaning three, aspirate-mutates the next word: ‘cant’ becomes ‘tri chant’.
‘yn’ before a place nasal-mutates it and itself becomes ‘yng’: ‘gogledd’ turns into ‘yng ngogledd’ for in the north.
‘peidio â’ means to stop or cease doing something: ‘wedi peidio â smocio’ = has stopped smoking.
‘fy’, meaning my, nasal-mutates the next word: ‘golwg’ becomes ‘fy ngolwg’.
‘ei’ meaning his leaves a following vowel unchanged: ‘ei ymroddiad’ = his dedication.
‘ers’ marks how long something has held up to now: ‘ers degawdau’ = for decades.
A feminine noun soft-mutates the adjective after it: ‘dwbl’ becomes ‘ddwbl’ in ‘enfys ddwbl’, since ‘enfys’ is feminine.
After ‘yn’ meaning in, a language name soft-mutates: ‘Cymraeg’ becomes ‘yn Gymraeg’ = in Welsh.
‘pe baen ni’ means if we had and opens an unreal condition, pairing with ‘byddai’ for would have.
‘wedi’ before a verb marks the perfect: ‘dw i wedi pasio’ = I have passed. Replace ‘wedi’ with ‘yn’ for I am passing.
An ‘oedd’ form plus ‘wedi’ is the past perfect: ‘oeddech chi wedi gorffen?’ = Had you finished?, one step back from the plain past.
‘wedi'i’ plus a softened verb says it has been done to the thing: ‘wedi'i ferwi’ (from ‘berwi’) = boiled.
For plural things use ‘wedi'u’, adding h before a vowel: ‘wedi'u hanfon’ (from ‘anfon’) = have been sent.
‘'n lân’, literally clean, works as an intensifier meaning completely: ‘wedi blino'n lân’ = worn out.
‘newydd’ plus a softened verb means just did: ‘newydd gyrraedd’ (from ‘cyrraedd’) = has just arrived. Use ‘wedi’ for the plain perfect.
Counting years uses ‘blynedd’, not ‘blwyddyn’, and it nasal-mutates to ‘mlynedd’ after five: ‘bum mlynedd’ = five years.
‘byddai’ plus ‘wedi bod’ is would have been: ‘byddai hi wedi bod yn braf’ = it would have been nice.
‘ers’ covers a span still going: ‘wedi byw ... ers pymtheng mlynedd’ = have lived for fifteen years and still do.
